sections.h2: What is Lincoln County, Missouri, and why has it grown so fast?
sections.html:
Lincoln County is an eastern Missouri county on the Mississippi River, across from Illinois, with Troy as its seat, and it belongs to the St. Louis metro area. It measures 640 square miles in total, 627 of them land. Pike, Calhoun (Illinois), St. Charles, Warren and Montgomery counties touch its edges.

The county dates from December 14, 1818 and honors Major General Benjamin Lincoln of the Revolutionary War. Its population went from 52,566 in 2010 to 59,574 in 2020, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 66,676, up 11.9% on the 2020 base.

The housing count tells the same story: 24,289 units in July 2025, and 252 building permits issued in 2025.

sections.h2: Which school districts and communities serve Lincoln County?
sections.html:
Wikipedia lists five districts based in or serving the county, and the levy of the one covering your address shows up on your bill. Lincoln County R-III in Troy is the biggest, running Troy Buchanan High School and New Horizons High School.

  • Lincoln County R-III (Troy), with Boone, Cuivre Park, Hawk Point and Main Street elementaries among others
  • Elsberry R-II
  • Silex R-I
  • Winfield R-IV
  • Wright City R-II, which covers the southern parts of the county

Moscow Mills, Old Monroe and Winfield sit in the southeast corner of the county, and Foley, Truxton and Whiteside are other named communities.

sections.h2: What do the Census figures say about Lincoln County households?
sections.html:
Homes here are valued at about $244,300 for owners in the 2020 to 2024 data, and 79.0% of households own. Income per household is $89,278 in 2024 dollars, and 7.9% of residents live in poverty.

sections.h2: Who sets and who bills Lincoln County property tax?
sections.html:
Kevin Bishop is the County Assessor, at 3 Front Street in Troy, and Jessica Zumwalt is the Collector of Revenue, at 1 Front Street. The Collector's taxpayer portal lists 636-528-0316 for the office and searches records by name, statement number or parcel number.

The Assessor's page breaks a bill into three parts. The assessor sets value, the taxing authority (a school, city or fire district) picks a rate from its budget, and the collector gathers the money. The Assessor has no hand in the rate.

The Collector's list of recipients is long: the state, county, ambulance, hospital, SB-40 board, county health center, schools, cities and fire districts. The same office takes drainage and neighborhood improvement district charges and merchant license fees, and it handles escrow payments from mortgage holders.

sections.h2: How are Lincoln County homes assessed?
sections.html:
A residential parcel is assessed at 19% of market value, farmland at 12% and commercial property at 32%. The Assessor revalues real estate in odd-numbered years such as 2021, 2023 and 2025, using a January 1 date, and checks for new or lost improvements in the even years between.

Field appraisers walk every parcel each year in marked county vehicles with ID badges. If someone without identification is on your land, the office asks you to call it. In a revaluation year the office compares recent sale prices with its own appraisals to decide whether land and buildings go up.

A change in value must come with a Notice of Change in Value. You may ask for an informal hearing, then go to the Board of Equalization, whose filing deadline is the second Monday in July. The board convenes on the third Monday in July, and the State Tax Commission follows it.

sections.h2: Which dates define the Lincoln County tax year?
sections.html:
Value is fixed on January 1 and payment is due on December 31, with several local dates in between. Transfers are posted to the new owner up to August 31, so a statement for a house sold after that date still goes out in the previous owner's name.

  • January 1: valuation date for real estate
  • Second Monday in July: appeal filing deadline for the board
  • Third Monday in July: the board convenes
  • Second week of July: the tax sale list starts running in the Lincoln County Journal and Elsberry Democrat
  • Fourth Monday in August, 10 a.m.: tax sale on the courthouse east steps
  • December 31: tax due

When a statement for a house you sold after August 31 reaches you, the Assessor's page says to ask the County Collector about forwarding it to the new owner. Compare the title company's closing statement to see how each side's share was credited.

sections.h2: What happens at the Lincoln County tax sale?
sections.html:
Real estate with three years of delinquent tax must be offered at the sale, which takes place on the fourth Monday in August at 10 a.m. on the courthouse's east steps. Owners may pay in full beforehand, and the collector says a high share do once the advertisement appears.

Bidders register from 8 a.m. in Room 103 of the courthouse, sign an affidavit saying they owe no delinquent tax, and must be present. A bidder who lives outside Missouri has to name a Lincoln County citizen as an agent. The opening bid covers the taxes, interest and charges.

The winner receives a certificate of purchase and pays the later taxes, but has no right to possession during the one-year redemption period. Any bid above the opening amount goes to the county treasurer for the owner of record, and money unclaimed after three years goes to the schools. The collector advises buyers to see an attorney first.

sections.h2: How do I pay or protest a Lincoln County bill?
sections.html:
Look up your bill on the Collector's taxpayer portal, call the office, or visit 1 Front Street in Troy. Searches accept a statement number such as R plus digits for real estate, a parcel number or an owner name, and the portal returns up to 100 records.

To protest a value, pay the full bill to the collector by December 31, mark the payment as a protest, and attach your reasons and the value you claim. A mailed payment needs a postmark of December 31 or earlier.

An attorney must file for an LLC, trust, estate or corporation. A taxpayer who never got notice of an increase, or who bought within 30 days of the statement mailing, may appeal straight to the State Tax Commission.

sections.h2: What should a Lincoln County seller check when taxes are owed?
sections.html:
Open your parcel record, request a written payoff from the Collector, and confirm that the Assessor shows the right owner and acreage. Ask which drainage, neighborhood improvement or other district charges appear on your bill.

  • Compare the statement with the title company's closing statement.
  • Ask whether any year is on the August tax sale list.
  • Ask the Collector about senior relief programs if the owner is an older homeowner.
  • If the sale closes after August 31, ask the Collector who will receive the statement.

The payoff comes out of the sale price at closing, so get the number in writing first.

faqs.q: Is Lincoln County property tax due December 31?
faqs.a: Yes. A mailed payment needs a postmark on or before that date to avoid penalty and interest.

faqs.q: On what date is the Lincoln County tax sale?
faqs.a: The fourth Monday in August, at 10 a.m. on the courthouse east steps in Troy. Bidder registration starts at 8 a.m. in Room 103.

faqs.q: How often is Lincoln County real estate revalued?
faqs.a: Every two years, in odd-numbered years such as 2025 and 2027, as of January 1. The even years pick up new construction and lost improvements.

faqs.q: When must I file with the Lincoln County Board of Equalization?
faqs.a: By the second Monday in July. The board convenes on the third Monday in July.

faqs.q: Which Lincoln County office do I call about a balance?
faqs.a: Call the Collector of Revenue at 636-528-0316. For a question about value, contact the Assessor at 3 Front Street in Troy.
